quote: No, actually the two formalisms in their most highly developed forms were proven equivalent.
content: They were not, and the people who built Minimum Message Length say so. Wallace and Dowe’s comparison (Wallace & Dowe (1999)) sets out the differences: MML works with an explicitly chosen model class and prior and is computable; Solomonoff induction is universal, defined relative to a reference machine, and uncomputable; they agree in their asymptotic behaviour on some problems and differ in others, and Wallace regarded the differences as substantive. There is also the point Book I’s annotations made about Solomonoff: the complexity of a theory is defined only up to an additive constant that depends on the choice of universal machine, and that constant can be made as large as one likes for any particular theory (Sterkenburg (2016)). So the essay’s demand that one “assign a number; and the number has to be meaningful, you can’t just make it up” is one the formalism cannot meet: the number it assigns is meaningful only relative to a machine one chose, and the choice is exactly where the two sides of an Occam dispute disagree. The formalism settles that objects are free and laws are costly, which is the point the essay needs; it does not settle how costly, which is the point the next essay needs.

quote: Occam’s Razor was raised as an objection to the suggestion that nebulae were actually distant galaxies—it seemed to vastly multiply the number of entities in the universe. All those stars!
content: Two essays earlier, in Belief in the Implied Invisible, the same episode was introduced with “though I failed to Google a source, I remember reading that.” Here it is stated as history. No source has been found by the annotator either; the island-universe debate from Kant and Wright through Curtis and Shapley in 1920 turned on distance measurements, on novae, and on van Maanen’s erroneous rotation data, and the surviving record of the Great Debate contains no appeal to parsimony against the number of stars. The essay needs a case in which Occam’s razor was misused to penalize a large universe, so that the misuse can be diagnosed as the one being made against many-worlds; lacking one, it promotes a half-remembered anecdote to a “part of the experimental evidence” for its account of simplicity. That is the pattern the annotations on Book I found in the history of science there, and it is worth naming when it appears inside an argument about what counts as evidence.

quote: Many-worlds is not a zillion worlds worth of complicated, any more than the atomic hypothesis is a zillion atoms worth of complicated. For anyone with a quantitative grasp of Occam’s Razor that is simply not what the term “complicated” means.
content: The point about worlds is correct, and it is the wrong point. The Everettian theory is not bare unitary evolution; bare unitary evolution predicts no frequencies at all. To touch experiment, the theory needs the Born rule, either as an additional postulate (a measure over branches) or as a derivation from further premises. As a postulate it is an extra law of exactly the kind the essay counts as costly, comparable in code length to the collapse rule it replaces, since both say “outcomes are weighted by squared modulus” and differ only in whether the unweighted branches persist. As a derivation, the Deutsch–Wallace decision-theoretic argument (Deutsch (1999); Wallace, The Emergent Multiverse, 2012) rests on rationality axioms that critics inside the Everett debate reject as question-begging (Kent, Albert and Price in Saunders et al., Many Worlds?, 2010), and the author of this sequence says in its final essay that he is “rather suspicious” of it. So the honest comparison is “unitary evolution plus Born measure” against “unitary evolution plus collapse with Born statistics,” and the code-length difference is not the one the essay computes. The essay proves that worlds are free and concludes that the theory is “strictly simpler”; the step between is where the Born rule went.
